selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence on which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters most. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components) is the simplest baseline in the space. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 that later changes can be measured against, one factor at a time: RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), adding images, multiprofile aggregation (avgpool, transformer), and fusion (concat, weighted). 3) With 9 experiments left, anchoring on a simple baseline first makes the following comparisons easier to interpret and guards against assuming that more complex multimodal setups will win. Next I would vary one dimension at a time, for example an image-only baseline or the multiprofile version of this RNA setup, before moving to the more complex combinations.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result so far. The single-profile RNA-only PCA baseline reached 0.536 accuracy and 0.516 F1. We know nothing yet about how informative the image modality is, and most of the remaining space (36 of 50 configurations) is multimodal and depends on it. 2. What this tests: an image-only, single-profile ResNet50 run gives a matched unimodal image baseline, with no aggregation or fusion. Comparing it directly with config_001 shows whether images are weaker than, comparable to, or stronger than RNA. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: this single clean comparison guides whether to prioritise multimodal fusion, image-encoder choices, or RNA-side improvements such as encoder and profile setting. It avoids changing several design choices at once while there is still too little evidence to exploit any direction.

1. Evidence: RNA-only with PCA (0.536 accuracy) far outperforms image-only with ResNet50 (0.227). RNA is the more informative modality, but only one profile setting has been tested. 2. Test: config_002 keeps the RNA-only model and pca_n2000 encoder fixed and changes only the profile setting, from singleprofile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation. This isolates whether multiprofile context helps on the strongest modality. 3. Why now: profile setting affects about two-thirds of the remaining search space. Using the simple avgpool aggregator gives a clean first test before trying transformer aggregation, other RNA encoders, or multimodal fusion.

1) Evidence: Multiprofile with avgpool aggregation raised RNA-only (pca_n2000) accuracy from 0.536 to 0.688, with F1 rising from 0.516 to 0.659. So profile aggregation looks like the strongest lever found so far. Image-only ResNet50 was weak at 0.227, so adding images is a lower-priority bet for now. 2) Test: config_003 keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer. This isolates whether a learned set-level aggregator gets more out of the multiple profiles than simple averaging. 3) Why now: it is a one-variable extension of the current best result, so it exploits the strongest evidence while answering a design question that shapes every later multiprofile experiment. The answer tells us which aggregator to carry into the remaining tests of RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT) and multimodal fusion, which keeps the remaining budget efficient.

1) Evidence: multiprofile avgpool aggregation is clearly the strongest direction so far. With pca_n2000, it reached 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. That beats single-profile (0.536) and transformer aggregation (0.512). Image-only ResNet50 is weak (0.227), so adding images is not yet a priority. The biggest untested factor is the RNA encoder, since only PCA has been tried. 2) Test: config_005 keeps the winning setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder to scvi_n200. This isolates whether a learned latent representation beats PCA. 3) Why now: it exploits the best known setup while resolving an important design choice with a single-variable change. Its result will decide whether later experiments, including multimodal fusion, should use PCA, scVI or scGPT next.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile PCA with avgpool (config_002, acc 0.688, F1 0.659). Avgpool clearly beat the transformer aggregator (0.512). PCA beat scVI under avgpool (0.688 vs 0.635). ResNet50 image-only single-profile was weak (0.227). The biggest open question is whether adding the image modality helps on top of the best RNA setup. 2. Test: config_019 keeps the winning RNA setup (PCA, multiprofile, avgpool) and only adds ResNet50 image features through weighted fusion. Weighted fusion should be able to downweight a weak image signal rather than dilute the RNA features, so this isolates whether images add useful complementary information. 3. Why now: With 4 experiments left, settling whether multimodal fusion helps decides how to spend the rest of the budget. If it helps, follow-ups could try concat fusion or the ViT-L image encoder. If it does not, the remaining runs can go to RNA-side options such as scGPT with avgpool (config_008).

1) Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile with avgpool and the PCA encoder (config_002, acc 0.688, F1 0.659). Avgpool clearly beat transformer aggregation (0.512). Switching to the scVI encoder lowered accuracy (0.635). Adding ResNet50 images with weighted fusion also did not help (0.650), which fits the weak image-only result (0.227). 1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile PCA with avgpool (config_002, 0.688 accuracy). Adding ResNet50 images with weighted fusion (config_019) lowered accuracy to 0.650. ResNet50 alone was very weak (0.227), so the weak image features may be what dragged the multimodal model down. Avgpool clearly beat the transformer aggregator, and PCA beat scVI and scGPT. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA, avgpool (config_002, acc 0.688, F1 0.659). Multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile. Avgpool beats transformer aggregation. PCA beats scVI and scGPT. Adding ResNet50 images with weighted fusion (config_019) fell to 0.650, and ViT-L images dropped further. The image modality alone is weak (0.227), so it is still unclear whether images hurt in general or whether weighted fusion is the problem. 2) Test: config_018 keeps everything from config_019 and changes only the fusion, from weighted to concat. This isolates the effect of fusion on the strongest RNA and image backbone combination. 3) Why now: Swapping weaker RNA encoders or using transformer aggregation is unlikely to beat 0.688. Concat fusion is the remaining untested change that could plausibly push past the RNA-only best. It also answers whether the fusion method, rather than the image modality, explains the multimodal drop. That leaves the final experiment for exploitation.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA, avgpool) at 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. Multiprofile with avgpool is clearly the strongest setting. Transformer aggregation, single-profile, scGPT, ViT-L and concat fusion all scored much lower. Weighted fusion with ResNet50 was the only multimodal setup that came close (0.650 with PCA). scVI avgpool RNA-only was the second-best RNA encoder at 0.635. 2. Test: This keeps the best aggregation (multiprofile avgpool) and the best fusion (weighted ResNet50). It swaps in scVI to see whether the image signal helps a compact, lower-dimensional RNA embedding more than it helped PCA, where it slightly hurt. 3. Why now: With one experiment left, only the best accuracy counts, so the pick should be an untested config that combines the strongest components. Every other untested option uses a component that clearly underperformed. This choice also answers whether the fusion benefit depends on the RNA encoder. It is unlikely to beat 0.688, so it is a modest bet on an encoder-by-fusion interaction rather than an expected improvement.

1) Evidence: RNA-only PCA single-profile (0.494 acc, 0.453 F1) beats ResNet50 image-only single-profile (0.411 acc, 0.378 F1). That makes RNA/PCA the strongest base so far. We have no data yet on profile setting, aggregation, fusion or the other encoders. 2) This experiment keeps the best-known base (RNA-only, pca_n2000) and changes one thing: single-profile becomes multi-profile, using simple avgpool aggregation. It shows whether pooling multiple profiles helps, which could affect every later configuration. 3) Profile setting is a key design axis, and this is the cleanest single-variable test of it on the strongest backbone. The result will tell us whether later experiments, including multimodal ones, should focus on multi-profile variants. Fusion and encoder comparisons can follow in the remaining budget.

1) Evidence so far: RNA beats image (0.494 vs 0.411 accuracy). Multiprofile avgpool gave a modest RNA gain (0.519 vs 0.494, with F1 also higher). Nothing has yet been tested on whether combining the two modalities helps, even though most of the remaining options are multimodal. 2) This run adds resnet50 image features, fused by simple concat, to the current best setup (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool). Only the image input changes, so the result directly shows whether image features add useful information beyond RNA or just add noise. 3) Fusion is the design choice with the largest untested potential upside and the most remaining options. Answering it now tells us whether the later budget should go to multimodal variants (ViT-L, weighted fusion, transformer aggregation) or stay with RNA-only encoder and aggregation choices.

Evidence: multiprofile avgpool beat singleprofile for RNA-only (0.519 vs 0.494). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion raised accuracy further to 0.535, with a clear F1 gain (0.519 vs 0.480). RNA is the stronger modality (0.494 vs 0.411 single-profile), yet only the PCA RNA encoder has been tested, so the RNA representation is the largest open uncertainty. This experiment keeps the best configuration (config_018) fixed and changes only the RNA encoder from PCA to scGPT, isolating the encoder's effect in the strongest setting. Because the dominant modality likely has the most leverage on accuracy, this is a better use of the remaining budget than first tuning fusion or aggregation. The result will guide whether later experiments exploit scGPT or test scVI and other dimensions on the PCA backbone.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_042 (multimodal, multiprofile, scGPT + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.591 accuracy and 0.573 F1. Moving from PCA to scGPT in that same setup gave a clear gain of about 0.055. The image modality looks weak on its own (ResNet50 image-only reached 0.411). That suggests the image representation may be a bottleneck. The alternative image encoder, ImageNet ViT-L, has never been tested, so this is a major unexplored design choice. 2. Test: Swap only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ViT-L and keep every other setting from config_042 fixed. This isolates the effect of the image representation within the current best setup. 3. Why now: The representation choice for one modality already produced the largest gain in this search. A stronger image encoder could plausibly give a similar improvement. Aggregation (transformer) and fusion (weighted) can still be refined in the remaining experiments on top of whichever image encoder wins.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_042 (scGPT + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.591 accuracy and 0.573 F1. Swapping the RNA encoder from PCA to scGPT gave about +5.5 points, while swapping the image encoder to ViT-L cost about 6 points. So scGPT with ResNet50 looks like the strongest backbone pair. Aggregation has never been varied: every multiprofile run used avgpool. Fusion has also never been varied: every multimodal run used concat. 2. This run keeps config_042 fixed and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. It tests whether learned attention over a cell's multiple profiles beats simple averaging, the largest untested design choice for this backbone. 3. It exploits the strongest backbone pair while still reducing uncertainty about one key factor. With 3 runs left, I can test weighted fusion next (config_043) and then combine whichever changes help (e.g., config_045).

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_044 (scGPT + ResNet50, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Switching from avgpool to transformer aggregation gave a large gain (0.591 to 0.715), and scGPT clearly beat PCA. ViT-L did worse than ResNet50 under avgpool, so changing the image encoder looks less promising. Fusion is the one design choice never tested: every multimodal run so far used concat. 2) Test: config_045 keeps the best configuration and changes only fusion from concat to weighted. This isolates the effect of the fusion method on the strongest backbone. 3) Why now: it exploits the best region of the search space while settling the last unexplored design factor with a single-variable change. With 2 experiments left after this one, the result will tell us which fusion to keep for any final refinement.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_044 (scGPT + ResNet50, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Transformer aggregation gave the largest single gain (+0.12 over avgpool). Concat fusion beat weighted fusion (0.715 vs 0.619). ResNet50 beat ViT-L (0.591 vs 0.530 under avgpool). The RNA encoder also mattered a lot: scGPT beat PCA by about 0.055 under avgpool. However, scVI has never been tested in any setting, so it is the largest remaining uncertainty among the important design choices. 2. Test: config_032 keeps the best setup fixed (ResNet50, multiprofile, transformer, concat) and swaps only the RNA encoder from scGPT to scVI. This isolates whether scVI's compact latent representation can match or beat scGPT. 3. Why now: With only two experiments left, this is the single-factor change most likely to beat 0.715 while also answering an open question. The other options look weaker. ViT-L and weighted fusion both already underperformed. An RNA-only transformer would mostly confirm whether images help rather than offer a likely new best. The final experiment can then exploit whichever RNA encoder wins.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_044 (scGPT + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Within that setup, transformer aggregation added about 0.12 over avgpool and concat beat weighted fusion. scVI and PCA RNA encoders were clearly weaker than scGPT. The one main untested question in the leading setup is the image encoder: ViT-L was worse than ResNet50 under avgpool (0.530 vs 0.591), but that is a single comparison and may not hold under transformer aggregation. 2) This run swaps only the image encoder (ResNet50 to ViT-L) while keeping scGPT, multiprofile, transformer aggregation and concat fusion. It tests whether attention-based aggregation makes better use of the higher-capacity ViT-L features. 3) As the last experiment, it changes one factor of the strongest setup, so the comparison is clean. It is also the remaining configuration with a credible chance of beating 0.715. The alternatives look less likely: an RNA-only scGPT transformer model drops the image signal, which helped slightly in the PCA comparison, and the PCA or scVI variants were weaker.

1. Evidence: no experiments have been run, so we do not yet know the relative value of the RNA encoder, the image encoder, multiprofile aggregation or multimodal fusion. 2. Test: an RNA-only, single-profile model with the simplest encoder (PCA, 2000 components) gives a low-complexity reference accuracy and F1. Later runs can then change one factor at a time against it: the encoder (scVI or scGPT), the profile setting (multiprofile with avgpool or transformer), the modality (image-only) or fusion. 3. 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far, RNA-only single-profile PCA at 0.650 accuracy and 0.628 F1. Nothing yet shows how informative the image modality is on its own. 2) This experiment runs the matched image-only single-profile baseline with the ResNet50 encoder. Holding the profile setting fixed while switching modality isolates how much signal images carry compared with RNA. 3) This is the most uncertain high-level design choice, and its answer shapes the rest of the budget. Starting from a single-profile baseline avoids changing several factors at once.

1) Evidence so far: two single-profile unimodal baselines exist. Image-only ResNet50 (acc 0.721, F1 0.681) beats RNA-only PCA (acc 0.650, F1 0.628). That is only one run per modality, so the gap is suggestive rather than conclusive. The main open question is whether RNA adds complementary signal to images or only dilutes the stronger modality. 2) config_016 adds the same PCA RNA encoder to the same ResNet50 image encoder, fused by simple concatenation, with single-profile input and no aggregation. Both encoders and the profile setting match the tested baselines, so any change against 0.721 can be attributed to combining the modalities. Concat is the simplest fusion and gives a clean reference point for a later comparison with weighted fusion. 3) Whether to pursue multimodal models is the largest structural branch of the search space; most of the remaining configurations are multimodal. Settling it now tells me how to spend the remaining 7 experiments: either exploit fusion further (weighted fusion, multiprofile aggregation, other encoders) or focus on image-only variants such as ViT-L and multiprofile aggregation.

Multimodal concat fusion did much worse (0.527), so naive fusion currently hurts. 2. Test: this run keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multi-profile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). Why now: it builds directly on the strongest result while answering a key design question with a single-variable change. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is single-profile image-only ResNet50 (acc 0.721, F1 0.681). RNA-only PCA is weaker (0.650). Concat fusion of the two dropped sharply to 0.527, below either unimodal model. So naive concatenation appears to hurt, but we do not yet know whether the fusion method is the cause or multimodality itself. Multiprofile avgpool (0.421) and ViT-L (0.411) both did poorly.

1) Evidence: Weighted fusion is the current best at 0.579 (config_017, pca_n2000 + resnet50, singleprofile), and concat fusion with the same encoders failed badly at 0.224. Separately, imagenet_vit_l beat resnet50 in the image-only singleprofile setting (0.535 vs 0.518), and multiprofile avgpool hurt resnet50 image-only (0.471). 2) config_023 keeps everything from the best configuration fixed and swaps only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l. It isolates whether the stronger image encoder's advantage carries over to weighted multimodal fusion. 3) This is the most direct exploitation of the strongest evidence with a single controlled change, and it is the likeliest to raise the best accuracy. That leaves 3 experiments to probe the RNA encoder (scvi/scgpt) or the profile setting around whichever multimodal configuration wins.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_023 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion) at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. Weighted fusion clearly beats concat (0.579 vs 0.224 with resnet50). ViT-L beats ResNet50 both alone and in fusion. Multiprofile avgpool hurt image-only ResNet50 (0.471 vs 0.518). The RNA encoder is the main untested choice: only pca_n2000 has been tried, and it is the weakest single modality (0.422). 2. Test: This swaps only the RNA encoder to scvi_n200 and keeps the best image encoder, single-profile setting and weighted fusion. Any change can then be attributed to the RNA representation, which could raise the multimodal ceiling if PCA is the bottleneck. 3. Why now: With two experiments left, a one-variable change to the top configuration is more likely to beat 0.713 than revisiting multiprofile aggregation, which has shown weak or negative evidence. The final experiment can then try scGPT, or exploit whichever RNA encoder wins.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_023 (PCA RNA + ViT-L image, single profile, weighted fusion) at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. Weighted fusion clearly beat concat (0.579 vs 0.224 with ResNet50). ViT-L beat ResNet50 both alone and when fused. Multiprofile avgpool hurt image-only accuracy (0.471 vs 0.518). Among RNA encoders, swapping PCA for scVI in the best setup dropped accuracy sharply (0.519). The scGPT encoder has not been tested anywhere and is the largest open question. 2. Test: config_047 keeps config_023 unchanged except for one factor, replacing PCA with scGPT. This shows directly whether a foundation-model RNA representation beats PCA in the strongest fusion setup. 3. Why now: The RNA encoder had the largest effect among the tested choices, so one more encoder swap could plausibly beat the 0.713 best. The alternative, multiprofile aggregation, already looked unfavorable with avgpool and would change more factors at once. With only two experiments left, this is the cleanest high-upside test, and the final run can then build on whichever RNA encoder wins.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_023 (PCA RNA + ViT-L image, single-profile, weighted fusion) at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. Weighted fusion clearly beat concat (0.579 vs 0.224 with ResNet50). ViT-L beat ResNet50 both alone and in fusion. PCA beat scGPT (0.635) and scVI (0.519) as the RNA encoder. The main open question is whether multiprofile input helps this winning setup. The only multiprofile result so far is weak evidence against it: avgpool lowered image-only ResNet50 from 0.518 to 0.471. Transformer aggregation has never been tested. 2. Test: This run keeps the best encoders and fusion fixed and changes only the profile setting, to multiprofile with transformer aggregation. A learned aggregator can weight informative profiles instead of averaging them, so it is the multiprofile option most likely to avoid the drop seen with avgpool. 3. Why this is the best last experiment: Only the best accuracy counts, so this run should exploit the top setup. Among single changes to config_023, this one has the most plausible upside. The alternatives look worse: switching to concat or a different encoder has already underperformed, and avgpool has a negative signal.

1. Evidence: No experiments have been run yet, so we know nothing about which modality, RNA encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion method works best. 2. What this tests: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components, no aggregation or fusion) is the simplest configuration. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 that every later change can be compared against. 3. Why now: With 10 experiments, a clean baseline makes the next steps easy to interpret. 1) Evidence: only one result exists, the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (acc 0.535, F1 0.519). Nothing is yet known about the image modality, which is a key design choice and a prerequisite for judging whether fusion is worth pursuing. 2) Test: config_010 is the simplest image-only setup (single-profile, ResNet50, no aggregation or fusion). It mirrors the RNA baseline, so it isolates the modality effect while holding profile setting, aggregation and fusion fixed. 3) Why now: knowing whether images carry comparable, weaker or stronger signal than RNA will steer the remaining 8 experiments, including how much budget to give multimodal fusion and which modality's encoder to tune. This makes it a better uncertainty-reducing step than changing the RNA encoder or profile setting next.

1) Evidence: The two single-profile baselines are close. RNA PCA reaches 0.535 accuracy and 0.519 F1, and image ResNet50 reaches 0.523 accuracy and 0.508 F1. Neither modality clearly dominates, so they may carry complementary information, but that has not been tested. 2) Test: config_016 combines exactly these two encoders (pca_n2000 + resnet50) with simple concat fusion in the single-profile setting. Comparing it to both baselines isolates the effect of adding a second modality, with no change to encoder, profile setting or aggregation. 3) Why now: Whether multimodal fusion helps is the biggest open design question, and it decides how much of the remaining 7 experiments should go to the large multimodal part of the space. If fusion gives no gain, I can shift to unimodal options such as multiprofile aggregation or other encoders.

1. Evidence: The three single-profile baselines score within about 1 point of each other: RNA PCA at 0.535, image ResNet50 at 0.523, and concat fusion at 0.532. Fusion has not beaten RNA alone, and F1 shows the same pattern. Profile setting is still completely untested and could be the most important design choice. 2. Test: config_002 keeps the best configuration so far (RNA-only, PCA) and changes only one thing, single-profile to multi-profile with simple average pooling. This isolates the effect of using multiple profiles. 3. Why now: Average pooling is the simplest aggregation, so the result reflects profile setting rather than aggregator complexity. The answer decides whether the remaining 6 experiments should go to the multi-profile half of the search space, which is larger, or to changing encoders in the single-profile setting.

1) Evidence so far: all four results fall in a narrow band (0.523–0.535 accuracy). The best is the simple RNA-only singleprofile PCA baseline (0.535). Adding images with concat fusion (0.532) did not beat it, and multiprofile avgpool (0.530) did not either. F1 follows the same ordering. Profile setting and concat fusion therefore look like weak levers so far. The largest untested factor is the representation itself: no alternative RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT) or image encoder (ViT-L) has been tried. 2) This experiment swaps only the RNA encoder, from PCA to scVI, in the best-performing setting (RNA-only, singleprofile). Because nothing else changes, any difference can be attributed to the RNA encoder. 3) Representation quality is the most likely source of a meaningful gain beyond the current plateau. RNA is currently the strongest modality, so improving its encoder could raise both unimodal and later multimodal configurations. With 5 experiments left after this one, the result will guide whether to try scGPT, ViT-L, or fusion and aggregation combinations built on the best encoder.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: All five results fall in a narrow band (0.523–0.535 accuracy, with F1 tracking accuracy). The best so far is RNA-only PCA single-profile at 0.535. Swapping PCA for scVI (0.532), adding images with concat fusion (0.532) and avgpool multiprofile (0.530) each gave small, likely non-significant drops. Image-only ResNet50 was the weakest (0.523). RNA looks like the strongest signal source, but representation quality may be the limiting factor, and scGPT is the main RNA encoder not yet tested. 2. What this tests: config_007 changes only the RNA encoder to scGPT, keeping the RNA-only single-profile baseline fixed. This cleanly isolates whether a foundation-model representation beats PCA and scVI. 3. Why now: Aggregation and fusion changes have not helped so far, so encoder quality is the most plausible remaining lever. A clean answer here decides how to use the last 4 experiments. If scGPT improves, extend it to multimodal or multiprofile variants (e.g., config_040/046/009). If not, test the ViT-L image encoder (config_013) or transformer aggregation with PCA.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: all six tested configurations fall in a narrow band of 0.523–0.536 accuracy. RNA encoders (PCA, scVI, scGPT) differ by under 0.005. Multiprofile avgpool and concat fusion gave no gain over single-profile RNA. Image-only ResNet50 is the weakest arm, and no tested configuration has changed the image encoder. 2. What this tests: config_013 swaps only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L in the single-profile image-only setting, so it cleanly isolates the effect of the image representation. 3. Why it is the best next use: a weak image representation may explain why concat fusion added nothing over RNA-only. If ViT-L clearly improves image accuracy, the remaining 3 experiments can go to ViT-L multimodal combinations (for example with scGPT or PCA). If it does not, the budget can shift to transformer aggregation or weighted fusion. Further RNA-encoder sweeps look unlikely to help.

1. Evidence: All strong results sit in a narrow band of about 0.530 to 0.536. RNA-only scGPT (0.5362) and RNA-only PCA (0.5353) are effectively tied. Concat multimodal (0.5321) and multiprofile avgpool (0.5305) did not help. The ViT-L image encoder is clearly worse. Two design choices remain untested: transformer aggregation and weighted fusion. 2. Test: config_003 keeps the strong PCA RNA-only setup and swaps avgpool for transformer aggregation in the multiprofile setting. Compared directly with config_002, this isolates whether learned attention over profiles can recover signal that simple averaging may wash out. 3. Why now: Transformer aggregation is the main untested lever that could plausibly move accuracy beyond the current plateau. If it works, the 2 remaining experiments can pair it with scGPT or with multimodal fusion. If it fails, the search can return to refining the single-profile setups.

1. Evidence: Single-profile RNA models lead and sit very close together (scGPT 0.536, PCA 0.535, scVI 0.532). Multimodal concat fusion with PCA and ResNet50 (0.532) did not beat RNA-only. Multiprofile aggregation never helped, and the transformer collapsed (0.328). The ViT-L image encoder is clearly weak (0.421). The main untested design choice is weighted fusion. Concat may let the weaker image features add noise, and weighted fusion could down-weight them. 2. Test: config_017 changes only the fusion method from config_016 (PCA + ResNet50, single profile, concat to weighted). This isolates whether weighted fusion lets multimodal models beat the best unimodal result. 3. Why now: Further RNA-only or multiprofile variants look unlikely to add much. This is the cleanest remaining comparison with real upside. If weighted fusion helps, the last experiment can apply it to the top RNA encoder (scGPT + ResNet50 weighted, config_041). If it does not, the final run can go to another option, such as scGPT + ResNet50 concat (config_040).

1) Evidence: weighted fusion of PCA RNA and ResNet50 image (config_017, 0.688 accuracy, 0.659 F1) is far ahead of every other run, including concat fusion with the same encoders (0.532). The other design choices matter much less. scGPT was the marginally best RNA encoder in unimodal tests (0.536 vs 0.535 for PCA). Multiprofile avgpool slightly hurt RNA (0.530), and the transformer aggregation failed badly (0.328). 2) This run keeps the winning setup of singleprofile, ResNet50 and weighted fusion, and changes only the RNA encoder from PCA to scGPT. It tests whether a pretrained RNA representation adds to the weighted-fusion gain. 3) With no experiments left, the best choice is exploitation: a one-factor change to the top configuration. That gives a reasonable chance of beating 0.688 and avoids choices like multiprofile aggregation, which previous results suggest are neutral or harmful.

1. No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion works best. 2. This tests the simplest configuration: RNA-only, single profile, PCA encoder, with no aggregation or fusion. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 that every more complex design must beat. 3. It is the best first use of the budget because later experiments can each change one factor from this anchor (encoder, image modality, multiprofile aggregation, fusion). That isolates each factor's effect instead of confounding several at once, and it avoids assuming that more complex multimodal models are better.

1) The only result so far is RNA-only, single-profile, PCA, at 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. Nothing is known yet about the image modality, which is a major design axis. 2) config_010 is the image-only, single-profile baseline with ResNet50. Keeping single-profile matches config_001, so this gives a direct comparison of how much signal each modality carries. 3) Knowing whether images are stronger, weaker or comparable to RNA will decide whether to spend the remaining budget on RNA encoders, image encoders or multimodal fusion. That makes it the best uncertainty-reducing experiment at this early stage, before committing to any complex configurations.

1. Evidence: The image-only ResNet50 single-profile model (0.635 accuracy, 0.618 F1) clearly beats the RNA-only PCA single-profile model (0.485 accuracy, 0.464 F1). This suggests image features carry most of the signal. It is still unknown whether RNA adds complementary information. 2. Test: config_016 keeps the exact same encoders (PCA RNA, ResNet50 image) and the single-profile setting, and combines them with simple concat fusion. It changes only one thing relative to the image-only baseline, the addition of RNA through fusion. Any gain or loss can therefore be attributed to multimodality rather than to a new encoder or profile setting. 3. Why now: Whether to pursue multimodal models decides how most of the remaining 7 experiments should be spent. A gain would open the multimodal branch. Concat is the simplest fusion baseline, so weighted fusion, multiprofile aggregation and encoder swaps can be explored afterwards. No gain would point the search toward image-only variants such as multiprofile aggregation and the ViT-L encoder.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Image features carry most of the signal (image-only 0.635 vs RNA-only 0.485). Adding PCA RNA with concat fusion gave a modest gain to 0.653, which is the current best. All three experiments so far used single profiles, so the effect of profile setting is completely untested. It could plausibly be a large effect. 2. What this tests: config_018 keeps the best configuration (PCA + ResNet50, concat) and changes only one thing, moving from singleprofile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation. This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles per sample improves accuracy. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: Profile setting is a high-impact, unexplored design choice. Testing it on the current best setup gives a clean one-variable comparison and a strong chance of a new best. If it helps, later experiments can compare transformer against avgpool aggregation, or swap encoders, within the multiprofile setting. If it does not help, the search can focus on encoders and fusion in the single-profile setting.

1. Evidence: Image features are the strongest signal so far. Image-only ResNet50 reached 0.635 accuracy, versus 0.485 for RNA-only PCA. Adding PCA RNA with concat fusion in the single-profile setting gave a modest gain to 0.653, the current best (F1 0.628). Multiprofile with avgpool performed much worse (0.519), so multiprofile is risky. Its transformer variants are still untested. 2. Test: This keeps the best configuration (single-profile, PCA RNA, concat) and changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. It isolates whether a stronger image representation improves the dominant modality. 3. Why now: Because image features drive most of the performance, the image encoder is the design choice most likely to move accuracy substantially. Changing one variable from the best setup exploits the strongest direction while keeping the comparison clean. RNA encoder, fusion type and transformer aggregation can be checked with the remaining five experiments.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_016 (single-profile, PCA RNA + ResNet50, concat fusion) at 0.653 accuracy. Image alone is fairly strong (0.635). RNA with PCA is weak (0.485), and adding it gives only a small gain. Two other directions did worse: avgpool multiprofile aggregation (0.519) and swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L (0.591). That points to RNA representation as the main untested factor that could raise the multimodal result. 2. Test: config_028 keeps config_016 exactly the same except for one change, using the scVI (200-dimension) RNA encoder instead of PCA. This shows whether a better RNA embedding adds more than PCA does on top of the strong ResNet50 image features. 3. Why now: This is a one-variable step from the current best, so the result is easy to read. It also probes RNA encoder choice, the largest design question still open. If scVI helps, the remaining budget can go to weighted fusion or scGPT; if not, fusion tuning on the PCA setup is the fallback.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_016 (single-profile, PCA RNA, ResNet50, concat fusion) at 0.653 accuracy and 0.628 F1, slightly above image-only ResNet50 at 0.635. Replacing ResNet50 with ViT-L, replacing PCA with scVI, or switching to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation all lowered accuracy. The fusion method is the one design choice not yet tested at all. 2. Test: config_017 keeps everything from config_016 and changes only concat to weighted fusion, so any difference isolates the effect of fusion on the strongest configuration. 3. Why now: With 3 experiments left, refining the current best along an unexplored axis is a direct chance to improve the top score. A clean one-factor comparison also tells the last runs whether weighted fusion should carry forward to other promising directions, such as transformer aggregation or the untested scGPT RNA encoder.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_016 (pca_n2000 + resnet50, singleprofile, concat) at 0.653 accuracy and 0.628 F1. Each single change away from it has lowered accuracy. Swapping in scvi_n200 gave 0.527, imagenet_vit_l gave 0.591, weighted fusion gave 0.512, and multiprofile with avgpool gave 0.519. RNA adds only a modest gain over image-only resnet50 (0.635), so a better RNA representation is the most plausible way to improve. The scGPT encoder is the main untested RNA option. 2. Test: config_040 keeps the best setup and changes only the RNA encoder to scGPT. This isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA embedding beats PCA in fusion. 3. Why now: With 2 experiments left, this one-variable change to the best configuration has a reasonable chance of beating 0.653. The alternative, transformer aggregation in multiprofile, is a riskier bet given how poorly multiprofile with avgpool did. If scGPT helps, the remaining budget can refine around it; if not, the transformer aggregation question can still be tested.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_016 (single-profile, PCA + ResNet50, concat fusion) at 0.653 accuracy. Changing almost any one design choice away from it has hurt. ViT-L, scVI, scGPT and weighted fusion all scored lower. The one design choice still untested is transformer aggregation. Multiprofile with avgpool (config_018) dropped sharply to 0.519, but that may reflect the simple pooling method rather than multiprofile input itself. 2. What this tests: config_020 changes only the aggregation from config_018, swapping avgpool for transformer. This isolates whether learned attention over profiles can recover or beat single-profile performance. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: It is the only remaining direction with a plausible chance of beating 0.653. The other untested options mostly use components already shown to underperform. If it fails, the final experiment can still try a nearby exploit.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_016 (single-profile PCA + ResNet50 with concat fusion) at 0.653. The image-only ResNet50 run nearly matches it at 0.635, so most of the signal appears to come from the image modality. Every change away from config_016 lowered accuracy: switching to scVI or scGPT, to ViT-L, or to weighted fusion all did worse. Multiprofile aggregation also dropped the multimodal model to about 0.52-0.53, but transformer aggregation did slightly better than avgpool (0.532 vs 0.519), and that drop may have been driven by aggregating the weaker RNA profiles. What this tests: whether transformer-based multiprofile aggregation helps when only the strong ResNet50 image features are aggregated. This is the one untested setting I would expect to plausibly beat 0.653. Why it is the best final pick: the other remaining options mostly extend choices that have already underperformed (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L, weighted fusion), so they have little realistic upside. Given the earlier multiprofile drops, this may still fall short, but it is the only remaining test of a design choice that has not yet been tried in isolation.

1. Evidence: no experiments have been run, so there is no information yet about which modality, RNA encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion works best. 2. Test: this runs the simplest configuration, RNA-only with a PCA (2000) encoder on a single profile, with no aggregation or fusion. It sets a baseline for validation accuracy and F1. 3. Why now: every later experiment can change one factor against this baseline. Planned comparisons are RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), image-only, multiprofile aggregation and multimodal fusion. Each step then shows its gain over a simple model, rather than assuming that more complex models are better.

1. Evidence: We have only one result so far. The RNA-only, single-profile, PCA baseline (config_001) reached 0.411 accuracy and 0.378 F1. That leaves every major design choice untested. 2. Test: config_002 changes one factor only, moving from single-profile to multi-profile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). RNA-only and the PCA encoder stay fixed, so any difference can be attributed to the profile setting. 3. Why now: Profile setting splits the search space roughly in half and affects every modality and encoder choice. Learning early whether aggregating multiple profiles helps will guide the remaining 8 experiments. Those can then compare transformer versus avgpool, the alternative encoders (scvi, scgpt) and the image and multimodal options.

1. Evidence: Going from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, holding the RNA encoder fixed at pca_n2000, raised validation accuracy from 0.411 to 0.530. F1 rose by a similar amount (0.378 to 0.515), so multiprofile is the strongest direction found so far. The biggest open question is whether adding the image modality helps at all. 2. Test: config_018 keeps config_002 unchanged (RNA pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and only adds a resnet50 image encoder with simple concat fusion. Any difference from config_002 can therefore be attributed to adding images, with no confound from aggregation or RNA encoder changes. 3. Why now: Whether to use images splits the remaining search space roughly in half, so answering it early best focuses the remaining 7 experiments. If images help, later runs can refine the image encoder, fusion and aggregation within the multimodal branch. If they do not, the budget can go to RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt) and transformer aggregation instead. It also builds directly on the current best configuration, so it has a real chance of improving the best accuracy.

1) Evidence so far: multiprofile clearly beat singleprofile for RNA-only PCA (0.530 vs 0.411 accuracy, with F1 agreeing). Adding ResNet50 image features with concat fusion lowered accuracy to 0.485. So the current best is RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool. The aggregation method has not been tested at all. 2) This experiment changes only avgpool to transformer, keeping everything else at the best configuration. It isolates whether a learned set-level aggregator gets more out of the multiprofile signal, which was the largest gain seen so far. 3) This is the best next use of the budget because aggregation applies to every multiprofile configuration, including future encoder and multimodal ones. Settling it now tells later experiments which aggregator to use. The RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT) can then be tested on top of the better aggregator.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile PCA with avgpool (config_002, acc 0.530, F1 0.515). Multiprofile clearly beat singleprofile (0.411). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.507, with a much lower F1 of 0.455). Adding ResNet50 images by concat fusion hurt (0.485). The RNA encoder is still untested: every run so far used PCA. 2) Test: This run keeps the best setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps PCA for scVI. That isolates the effect of the RNA representation. 3) Why now: The encoder is the largest remaining uncertainty on the strongest branch. A single-variable change from the best configuration is the most direct way to raise the best accuracy. If scVI wins, the remaining budget can build on it, for example by checking scGPT or revisiting fusion with a stronger RNA encoder.

1. Evidence: The RNA encoder is the largest effect seen so far. Swapping pca_n2000 for scvi_n200 in the multiprofile avgpool RNA-only setting raised accuracy from 0.530 to 0.619, with F1 rising from 0.515 to 0.610. Multiprofile avgpool also beat single-profile and transformer aggregation with PCA. Adding resnet50 images with concat fusion lowered accuracy (0.485). The third encoder option, scgpt, has not been tested at all. 2. Test: config_008 keeps the best-performing setting (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder to scgpt. This directly tells us whether scgpt beats scvi_n200. 3. Why now: The encoder choice gave the biggest gain so far, and scgpt is the main untested option on that axis. With 4 experiments left, settling it now tells us which encoder to carry into later aggregation or multimodal tests, so those experiments start from the strongest base.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is scVI multiprofile avgpool (config_005, 0.619 accuracy, 0.610 F1). It beats scGPT (0.586) and PCA (0.530). Multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile. Transformer aggregation underperformed avgpool with PCA. Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion hurt PCA (0.485 vs 0.530). It is unclear whether that drop came from the image modality itself or from naive concat fusion. 2) Test: config_031 keeps the best RNA setup (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds ResNet50 with weighted fusion. Weighted fusion can learn to down-weight a weak modality, so this shows whether images add value on top of the strongest RNA representation once fusion is not forced to treat both modalities equally. 3) Why now: it is the smallest extension of the current best. It reuses the only image encoder already tested, so the result can be compared against both config_005 and the PCA concat result. Its outcome will decide how to spend the last 3 experiments: if it helps, try ViT-L or transformer variants; if it does not, return to tuning RNA-only scVI, for example transformer aggregation in config_006.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only scVI with avgpool (config_005, 0.619 acc, 0.610 F1). scVI beat scGPT and PCA, and avgpool beat transformer aggregation with PCA. Adding ResNet50 images lowered accuracy in both multimodal runs (PCA concat 0.485 vs 0.530; scVI weighted 0.535 vs 0.619). Image encoder choice is the main untested factor: ViT-L has never been tried. 2) Test: config_037 keeps the strongest RNA setup (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool) and the weighted fusion already tried with scVI. It changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ViT-L. This directly compares against config_031 and shows whether the drop from adding images came from weak ResNet50 features or from adding images at all. 3) Why now: Aggregation looks settled toward avgpool, so a scVI transformer run is less likely to set a new best. A stronger image representation is the most plausible way to beat 0.619, and weighted fusion should let the model reduce reliance on images if they add little. If this run also underperforms, the last two experiments can go to RNA-only refinements.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile scVI with avgpool (config_005, 0.619 acc, 0.610 F1). scVI beat scGPT and PCA under the same setting. Multiprofile clearly beat singleprofile. Adding images has lowered accuracy every time (PCA concat 0.485 vs 0.530 RNA-only; scVI weighted 0.535 and ViT-L weighted 0.512 vs 0.619 RNA-only). The aggregation method is the main untested choice for the best encoder. Transformer aggregation has been tried only with PCA, where it scored slightly lower (0.507 vs 0.530) on a single comparison. That may not carry over to the more compact scVI embeddings. 2. Test: config_006 changes only the aggregation (avgpool to transformer) relative to the current best. It shows whether learned aggregation over profiles can push the strongest representation higher. 3. Why now: With two experiments left, a one-variable change from the best configuration is the most promising way to beat it. More multimodal variants look unlikely to help given the consistent drops. If config_006 falls short, the last experiment can still target another refinement.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is the RNA-only, multiprofile scVI encoder with avgpool (config_005: 0.619 accuracy, 0.610 F1). Several other choices consistently did worse. Transformer aggregation lowered accuracy for both PCA and scVI. Singleprofile lowered it for PCA. Adding images also lowered it. The scVI weighted-fusion models fell to 0.535 with ResNet50 and 0.512 with ViT-L. The one untested piece of the scVI multimodal design is the fusion method itself. With PCA features, concat fusion (0.485) cost less relative to RNA-only (0.530) than weighted fusion did with scVI. 2. Test: config_030 changes only the fusion method relative to config_031 (concat instead of weighted, keeping scVI, ResNet50 and avgpool). It checks whether the weighted-fusion design caused the multimodal drop, or whether adding the image modality hurts regardless of fusion. 3. Why this is the best final experiment: the remaining RNA-only options combine settings that already underperformed (singleprofile, or scGPT with transformer), so they are unlikely to beat 0.619. config_030 builds on the strongest RNA setup and is the remaining option with a plausible, if modest, chance of improving on it. It also isolates one design choice cleanly.

1) No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about which modality, RNA encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion works best. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, lowest-variance setup in the space. It sets a reference point, and every later choice can be judged as a single change from it: scVI or scGPT for the encoder, multiprofile for the profile setting, image-only for the modality, or adding fusion. 3) With 10 runs for 51 configurations, a clean anchor makes the next experiments easy to read. Each one can isolate one design factor rather than leaving us to untangle several changes at once from an initial complex run.

1) Evidence: the image-only ResNet50 single-profile model is the best so far (acc 0.532, F1 0.516). Its F1 lead over every RNA-based run is clearer than its small accuracy lead. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is single-profile ResNet50 image-only (acc 0.532, F1 0.516). Single-profile PCA RNA-only scores 0.519. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is image-only ResNet50 single-profile (0.532 accuracy, 0.516 F1). PCA RNA is close behind (0.519). 1) Evidence: The RNA encoder is the strongest factor found so far. scGPT single-profile RNA-only reached 0.586 accuracy and 0.574 F1, well above PCA (about 0.519) and ResNet50 image-only (0.532). Multiprofile avgpool did not help either PCA RNA or ResNet50 images. Weighted fusion hurt badly (0.435). Concat is the fusion method least likely to hurt, and ResNet50 is the best image encoder tested. That makes this the most plausible single step to beat 0.586.

Evidence: scGPT RNA-only single-profile (config_007, acc 0.586, F1 0.574) is clearly the best result so far. It beats PCA RNA-only (~0.52), every ResNet50 image-only run (≤0.532) and every multimodal fusion run (≤0.520). Adding images to scGPT reduced accuracy (config_040, 0.507), so further multimodal tests look unpromising. Multiprofile avgpool gave essentially no change for PCA (0.518 vs 0.519) and a slight drop for ResNet50 (0.523 vs 0.532). That suggests simple mean pooling is unlikely to add much on top of scGPT. Transformer aggregation has never been tested and is the main open question on the profile and aggregation axis. Test: config_009 keeps the best encoder (scGPT) and changes only the profile setting and aggregation, to see whether learned attention over multiple profiles can beat single-profile scGPT. Why it is the best use of the last experiment: only the best accuracy counts, and config_007 is already secured. A higher-variance extension of the strongest direction is therefore preferable to config_008 (avgpool), whose expected gain from prior evidence is near zero. It is also preferable to scVI or ViT-L options, which have no supporting evidence or performed poorly.

1. No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about any design choice: modality, RNA or image encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion. 2. 1. Evidence: RNA-only single-profile with PCA (0.678 acc, 0.646 F1) is the current best. Multiprofile avgpool was slightly worse (0.653). 1. Evidence: PCA RNA-only single-profile (config_001, 0.678) is the clear leader. scVI and scGPT were much worse, and multiprofile avgpool (0.653) gave no gain. The one multimodal run, PCA + ResNet50 with concat fusion (config_016), collapsed to 0.224, far below RNA alone. A drop that large points to a fusion problem, such as the image features swamping or adding noise to the RNA signal, rather than to images carrying no information. 2. Test: config_017 keeps everything from config_016 and changes only the fusion, from concat to weighted. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only singleprofile PCA (0.678 accuracy, 0.646 F1). PCA clearly beats scVI and scGPT. Multiprofile pooling did not help, with avgpool slightly worse and the transformer collapsing. In multimodal runs, weighted fusion was far more stable than concat (0.635 vs 0.224), but adding ResNet50 images still fell short of RNA alone. 2) Test: keep the strongest settings fixed (PCA, singleprofile, weighted fusion) and change only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only PCA singleprofile (0.678 accuracy). PCA clearly beats scVI and scGPT. Transformer aggregation and concat fusion both collapse to about 0.22. Weighted fusion keeps multimodal models competitive: 0.635 with ResNet50 and 0.599 with ViT-L, and ResNet50 does better. Multiprofile with avgpool costs only a little (0.653 against 0.678). It reuses only components that have already worked and avoids the failed transformer and concat options. Why now: the other untested options are unlikely to exceed 0.678. Those include image-only models, the weaker RNA encoders, and anything with transformer aggregation or concat fusion. This makes config_019 the most plausible candidate to beat the current best, and it tells us whether the final experiment should continue down this multimodal multiprofile direction.

Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only PCA single-profile (0.678). Every multimodal variant has fallen below it. Weighted fusion is clearly needed, since concat collapsed to about 0.22. Transformer aggregation also collapsed (0.227), which makes it a high risk on the final run. The scVI and scGPT encoders were much weaker than PCA. The only untested configurations that pair PCA with weighted fusion are 021 and 027, both transformer-based, and 025. This experiment tests whether ViT-L image features with multiprofile avgpool and weighted fusion beat ViT-L single-profile weighted (0.599). That would show whether profile pooling helps the ViT image branch. Multiprofile avgpool with ResNet50 and weighted fusion (0.629) stayed close to its single-profile counterpart (0.635), so a similar small effect is plausible here. This choice avoids the components that failed (concat, transformer) and the weak RNA encoders. It is still unlikely to beat 0.678, but it is the most plausible remaining candidate and also closes a gap in the ViT-L design comparison.

1. Evidence: The image-only model (0.471) clearly beat RNA-only (0.332). What this tests: config_007 changes only the encoder to scGPT within the best-performing RNA-only single-profile setting. That cleanly completes the three-way RNA encoder comparison. 3. Why now: the RNA branch is so far the strongest signal, and a better encoder could beat the current best directly. The result would also tell us which encoder to carry into the remaining multiprofile-transformer or fusion experiments. This makes it a good balance of exploitation and closing a key open question.

1) Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. scGPT single-profile reached 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1, far above PCA (0.540), scVI (0.525), ResNet50 image-only (0.512) and PCA+ResNet50 concat fusion (0.507). Multiprofile with avgpool slightly hurt PCA (0.540 to 0.520), and transformer aggregation has never been tested. 2) This experiment keeps the best encoder, scGPT, and changes only the profile setting, using transformer aggregation. It tests whether learned attention over multiple profiles adds signal on top of strong scGPT embeddings, where simple averaging did not help PCA. 3) Three experiments remain, so the priority is building on the scGPT result. Transformer aggregation has more upside than avgpool, which already showed a small loss. Adding images is riskier because they have contributed little so far. If this beats 0.715, the remaining budget can refine multiprofile scGPT. If not, I can switch to scGPT multimodal with weighted fusion.

1) Evidence: scGPT single-profile RNA (config_007, 0.715 acc / 0.687 F1) beats every other run by about 0.17 accuracy. Multiprofile setups did worse for both PCA (0.540 to 0.520) and scGPT (0.715 to 0.537), so multiprofile looks unpromising. Concat fusion of PCA with ResNet50 also lowered accuracy versus RNA-only (0.540 to 0.507), but weighted fusion has never been tested. 2) Test: this adds ResNet50 image features to the strong scGPT single-profile model using weighted fusion, which can learn to down-weight the weaker image branch. It changes only the modality and fusion relative to the best run and keeps the image encoder already characterized (ResNet50 image-only, 0.512). 3) Why now: with two experiments left, the best chance of beating 0.715 is to build on the scGPT single-profile winner. Weighted fusion is the option most likely to avoid the loss seen with concat. If it helps, the final run can try ViT-L or concat; if it hurts, we will know the best model is likely the RNA-only one.

1) Evidence: scGPT single-profile RNA-only (config_007) is the clear leader at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Every added complexity around scGPT has hurt it so far. Multiprofile with transformer aggregation (config_009) collapsed it to 0.537. Adding a ResNet50 image branch with weighted fusion (config_041) dropped it to 0.573. For PCA, multiprofile avgpool cost only about 0.02 accuracy versus single-profile, so the scGPT collapse may come mostly from the transformer aggregator rather than from multiprofile itself. 2) This experiment keeps the scGPT encoder fixed and swaps only the aggregator from transformer to avgpool. That isolates whether the multiprofile setting or the transformer aggregator caused the drop. 3) Image encoders have so far contributed little, and multimodal fusion has consistently underperformed RNA-only. Among the untested options, this simple, low-variance aggregation is the most plausible way to match or exceed 0.715. It also tells the final experiment whether to keep pursuing multiprofile scGPT variants or to explore elsewhere.

1. Evidence: scGPT is clearly the strongest RNA encoder. Singleprofile RNA-only scGPT (config_007) is the best result so far at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Multiprofile aggregation hurt scGPT (avgpool 0.635, transformer 0.537). Adding ResNet50 images through weighted fusion also hurt (0.573), so ResNet50 appears to add noise. The ImageNet ViT-L image encoder has never been tested, so whether a stronger image representation helps is the main open question. 2. Test: this run keeps the best RNA setting (scGPT, singleprofile) and weighted fusion, which kept accuracy and F1 more balanced than concat did. It swaps only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ViT-L, isolating whether a better image representation lets multimodal fusion beat RNA-only. 3. Why this run: with one experiment left, only beating 0.715 matters. The untested multiprofile or non-scGPT options are unlikely to win given the evidence so far. This configuration is the most plausible remaining upside, though it may still fall short of RNA-only scGPT.

1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion works best. 2) This run sets a simple reference point: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA (2000 components), with no aggregation or fusion. Each later run can then change one design choice at a time against it. Planned comparisons include adding multiprofile aggregation, switching to scVI or scGPT encoders, trying image-only models and adding image fusion. 3) A cheap, interpretable baseline is the best first use of the budget. It lets the 9 remaining experiments measure whether added complexity actually improves validation accuracy, rather than assuming multimodal or multiprofile models are better.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: There is only one result so far. The RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_001) reached 0.629 validation accuracy and 0.599 F1. We know nothing yet about how profile setting, encoder choice or modality affect performance. 2) What this tests: config_002 changes one factor from the baseline. It moves from single-profile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation, keeping the RNA-only setting and PCA encoder fixed. Any accuracy change can therefore be credited cleanly to multiprofile input with the simplest aggregation. 3) Why now: profile setting affects most of the remaining search space, since most untested configurations are multiprofile. Learning early whether multiprofile helps lets later experiments prune or focus large groups of configurations. Using avgpool first gives a low-complexity reference that a transformer-aggregation test could build on later. Encoder and modality comparisons, such as scVI/scGPT or image-only, remain natural follow-ups.

1. Evidence: with the PCA RNA encoder held fixed, singleprofile (0.629 accuracy, 0.599 F1) clearly beat multiprofile with avgpool (0.507 accuracy, 0.455 F1). That is a large gap, but it is one comparison. It is unclear whether multiprofile itself hurts or whether simple average pooling washes out per-profile signal. 2. Test: config_003 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, keeping rna_only, multiprofile and pca_n2000 fixed. This isolates whether learned attention-based aggregation can recover or beat singleprofile performance. 3. Why now: most remaining configurations, including most multimodal ones, are multiprofile. Settling whether multiprofile is viable with a better aggregator tells us whether to prune or pursue a large part of the space, which makes the remaining 7 experiments more efficient than testing encoders or images first.

1) Evidence: with PCA RNA, singleprofile (0.629 acc, 0.599 F1) clearly beat multiprofile avgpool (0.507) and transformer (0.421). This is a consistent pattern, though it was seen with only one encoder. The image modality is completely untested, and that is the largest remaining uncertainty since roughly two-thirds of the search space involves images. 2) config_010 tests image-only singleprofile with ResNet50. It keeps the best-performing profile setting fixed and changes only the modality, so it shows whether images alone are competitive with the 0.629 RNA baseline. 3) Under the remaining budget, learning whether the image signal is strong or weak decides whether to put later runs into multimodal fusion or into RNA encoder alternatives (scVI, scGPT). That makes it more informative than another RNA encoder swap now.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is single-profile RNA with PCA (0.629 accuracy). Image-only ResNet50 single-profile is weaker but not trivial (0.485), so images may carry useful signal. Multiprofile aggregation clearly hurt RNA, with avgpool at 0.507 and transformer at 0.421. 2) Test: This adds the ResNet50 image features to the best RNA setup using simple concat fusion, keeping single-profile and PCA fixed. Only the image modality changes, so the result shows whether image information adds to RNA. 3) Why now: The open question with the largest possible gain is whether fusing modalities beats the RNA-only baseline. Its answer decides how to spend the remaining 5 experiments: exploring fusion type and image encoder (ViT-L), or going back to RNA-only encoders (scVI, scGPT). Concat is the simplest fusion and a clean first probe.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only single-profile with PCA (config_001, 0.629 accuracy). Multiprofile aggregation hurt RNA performance (0.507 with avgpool, 0.421 with transformer). Image-only was weaker (0.485). Concat fusion with ResNet50 fell below RNA alone (0.536). The RNA encoder is the main untested choice, because every RNA run so far used PCA. 2. Test: Swapping PCA for scVI in the best setup (RNA-only, single-profile) changes only the encoder, so it directly measures whether a learned latent representation improves on the strongest baseline. 3. Why now: The RNA branch drives performance, so improving it is the most likely route to a higher best accuracy. It would also guide any later multimodal runs. The remaining budget still allows a scGPT comparison (config_007) and a follow-up on whichever encoder wins.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is single-profile RNA-only with PCA (config_001, 0.629 accuracy). Multiprofile aggregation hurt RNA-only (0.507 with avgpool, 0.421 with transformer). Image-only was weaker (0.485), and concat fusion with resnet50 fell below RNA-only (0.536). Switching the RNA encoder to scVI also lowered accuracy (0.532). So the RNA representation strongly drives performance, but the scGPT encoder is still untested. 2. Test: config_007 keeps the best setting (RNA-only, single-profile, no aggregation, no fusion) and changes only the RNA encoder to scGPT. This cleanly finishes the encoder comparison. 3. Why now: the RNA encoder is the most important open choice, and a pretrained foundation-model embedding could plausibly beat PCA.
