1) Evidence: The best result so far is single-profile RNA-only PCA (0.629 accuracy, 0.599 F1). Multiprofile aggregation clearly hurt (0.42-0.51). The scVI and scGPT encoders underperformed PCA. Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion fell to 0.536, below RNA alone, probably because the weaker image features (0.485 on their own) dilute the RNA signal under naive concatenation. 2) Test: config_017 changes only the fusion method from config_016, from concat to weighted. This shows whether a learned modality weighting can protect the strong RNA signal while adding useful image information, which is the main untested way multimodal models could beat 0.629. 3) Why now: Single-profile PCA is the clear winner, so remaining experiments should stay in that setting. Multiprofile variants have little upside. Changing just one variable keeps the result interpretable. If weighted fusion helps, a remaining slot can test PCA plus ViT-L with weighted fusion (config_023). If it does not, a slot can check whether ViT-L image features (config_013) are stronger than ResNet50.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only single-profile PCA (config_001, 0.629 acc / 0.599 F1). The multiprofile variants underperformed it, as did the scVI and scGPT RNA encoders. Concat fusion with ResNet50 lowered accuracy to 0.536, probably because ResNet50 image features are weak (0.485 image-only). Weighted fusion was much worse (0.328). The main untested factor is the stronger ImageNet ViT-L image encoder. 2. Test: config_022 keeps the best RNA setup (PCA, single-profile) and concat fusion, and swaps only ResNet50 for ViT-L. Compared directly with config_016, this isolates whether better image features make fusion add value instead of hurting. 3. Why now: With only two experiments left, this is the one remaining direction that both answers an important design question and has a plausible chance of beating 0.629. Testing ViT-L image-only would answer the encoder question but is very unlikely to beat the RNA baseline itself. Multiprofile and alternative RNA encoders have consistently underperformed, so they are poor bets.

1) Evidence: single-profile RNA-only PCA is the best result so far (0.629). Multiprofile aggregation clearly hurt PCA (0.507 with avgpool, 0.421 with transformer). Weighted fusion and the ViT-L image encoder also performed poorly. Concat fusion with ResNet50 was the least harmful multimodal choice (0.536). Among RNA encoders, scGPT was second best (0.573) and had the most balanced F1 (0.573), suggesting a robust representation. 2) Test: this run checks whether scGPT pairs better with ResNet50 image features than PCA did under the least harmful fusion setup, concat in single-profile mode. That isolates the RNA-encoder-by-fusion interaction. 3) Rationale: this is the last experiment, so the goal is the best remaining chance of beating 0.629. Every other untested option uses a component that has already performed poorly (multiprofile aggregation, ViT-L or weighted fusion). This configuration avoids all of them while testing an untried combination. It is unlikely, but plausible, that it exceeds the PCA baseline.

1. There is no evidence yet, so every design choice is uncertain: modality, profile setting, RNA and image encoder, aggregation, and fusion. 2. This run sets a mid-complexity anchor: multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA plus ResNet50 image features, average pooling and concat fusion. Each component is the simplest option within its type. Almost every single-factor ablation is available next: RNA-only (config_002), image-only (config_011), single-profile (config_016), transformer aggregation (config_020), weighted fusion (config_019), and alternative RNA or image encoders (config_030, config_024). 3. With only 10 runs, a central configuration that can plausibly score well gives a baseline to compare against. It lets the next experiments isolate one factor at a time, rather than starting from the weakest corner of the search space.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: We have only one result. The multimodal, multiprofile configuration (PCA RNA + ResNet50 image, avgpool, concat) reached 0.421 accuracy and 0.412 F1. That gives a baseline but says nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2. What this tests: config_024 keeps everything the same except the image encoder, swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. Because only one factor changes, any difference can be attributed to the image representation. 3. Why it is the best next use of the budget: The image encoder is one of the main representation choices, and a stronger pretrained encoder could plausibly raise accuracy. If ViT-L helps, later experiments can build on it; if it does not, we keep ResNet50 and move on to other factors such as RNA encoder, aggregation or profile setting. A modality ablation (RNA-only, config_002) would also have been reasonable, since we do not yet know how much the image branch contributes. That remains a useful check later.

1) Evidence: with everything else held fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool, concat), switching the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l raised validation accuracy from 0.421 to 0.639, and F1 rose similarly. That makes the image encoder the strongest signal so far. Aggregation, fusion, RNA encoder and the value of multiprofile input are all still untested. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration (config_024) and changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer. It tests whether learned attention across multiple profiles beats simple mean pooling when paired with the stronger image features. 3) It is a single-factor change around the current best, so it can both improve the result and cleanly isolate an important design choice. Later experiments can test fusion (weighted), RNA encoders (scvi or scgpt) and image-only or single-profile baselines against this anchor.

1) Evidence: The image encoder matters a lot. Swapping resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l raised accuracy from 0.421 to 0.639, and F1 rose with it. Under vit_l, avgpool clearly beat transformer aggregation (0.639 vs 0.485). The RNA encoder is still completely untested: every run so far used pca_n2000. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration (config_024: multiprofile, vit_l, avgpool, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder, from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200. That isolates the effect of the RNA representation. 3) RNA encoder is the largest unexplored design dimension, with three options. A single-variable test against the current best both reduces that uncertainty and could directly beat 0.639. If scvi helps, scgpt (config_048) is the natural next comparison. If it does not, later runs can refine fusion (weighted, config_025) on the pca setup or check RNA's contribution with image-only vit_l (config_014).

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_024 (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + concat) at 0.639 accuracy and 0.620 F1. Three single-factor changes from it each hurt badly. Swapping to resnet50 gave 0.421. Swapping to transformer aggregation gave 0.485. Swapping to scvi_n200 gave 0.260. Fusion is the one design choice not yet tested. 2. Test: config_025 changes only concat to weighted fusion and keeps everything else from the best configuration. This isolates the effect of fusion. The large scVI drop suggests the way RNA and image signals are combined matters a lot, so a learned weighting could balance the modalities better than concatenation. 3. Why now: This is the most direct, low-risk extension of the strongest configuration. It resolves an untested design axis and has a real chance of beating 0.639. Five experiments remain after it, leaving room to later check image-only or scgpt variants.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_025 (PCA RNA, ViT-L image, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Three choices look consistent: ViT-L clearly beat ResNet50 under concat, avgpool beat transformer aggregation, and weighted fusion beat concat by about 8 points. The RNA encoder is still uncertain. scVI was much worse than PCA (0.26 vs 0.64 under concat), and scGPT has never been tested. 2. Test: This keeps the best image encoder, aggregation and fusion and changes only the RNA encoder to scGPT. It shows directly whether a foundation-model RNA embedding beats PCA in the strongest setup. 3. Why now: The RNA encoder is the main untested design axis that could raise the top score. Changing one variable from the best configuration keeps the comparison clean. With 4 experiments left, it is a reasonable bet: a cheaper check than broad exploration, with real upside if scGPT outperforms PCA.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_025 (PCA_n2000 + ViT-L, multiprofile avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.721 accuracy. Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L raised accuracy by about 0.22, while scVI and scGPT RNA encoders both performed much worse than PCA. This suggests the image representation carries much of the signal. Weighted fusion beat concat by about 0.08, which may mean the model gains from down-weighting a weaker RNA branch. The main open question is whether RNA adds anything beyond ViT-L image features. This experiment runs the image-only model with ViT-L and multiprofile avgpool, which changes only the model setting relative to the best configuration. It shows whether multimodality truly helps or whether image-only could match or beat 0.721. With 3 experiments left, settling this modality question first decides where the remaining budget goes: refining multimodal fusion and profile setting, or exploiting image-only variants.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_025 (PCA RNA, ViT-L image, multiprofile avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Weighted fusion beat concat on this setup (0.721 vs 0.639). ViT-L clearly beat ResNet50, and PCA clearly beat scVI and scGPT. Transformer aggregation hurt (0.485 vs 0.639 with concat). The singleprofile setting has never been tested, so it is the largest open uncertainty. 2. Test: config_023 keeps the best configuration's RNA encoder, image encoder and weighted fusion, and changes only the profile setting to singleprofile. This isolates whether multiprofile aggregation actually helps, or whether avgpool over profiles dilutes the signal. 3. Why now: Retrying the transformer (config_027) or ResNet (config_019) is unlikely to pay off given the poor results for both. This single-variable change has a real chance of beating 0.721. Either way, the result tells me how to use the final two experiments.

1. Evidence: the best result is config_025 (PCA-2000 + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.721 accuracy. Image-only ViT-L with the same profile setting and aggregation reached only 0.532, and the concat version of the multimodal model reached 0.639. So the PCA RNA features seem to drive much of the gain, especially when weighted fusion can adjust how much each modality counts. The main untested question is how well RNA does on its own: no RNA-only model has been run. The other candidate extensions look weak. The transformer aggregator cut accuracy sharply (0.639 to 0.485), ResNet50 underperformed ViT-L, and scVI and scGPT were much worse than PCA. 2. Test: config_002 isolates the PCA RNA representation under the best profile and aggregation settings (multiprofile, avgpool), with no image branch. This shows whether the image branch adds value or whether RNA alone can match or beat the multimodal model. 3. Why now: this removes the largest remaining uncertainty and has a realistic chance of a new best. It also leaves one experiment to exploit whichever direction wins, either refining the multimodal model or pursuing RNA-only.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_025 (PCA-2000 + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Weighted fusion beat concat by about 0.08 accuracy with the same backbone (0.721 vs 0.639). The other alternatives look weaker under concat: scVI (0.260) and ResNet50 (0.421). scGPT was also weak even with weighted fusion (0.427). The main open question is aggregation. Transformer aggregation hurt under concat (0.485 vs 0.639), but it has never been tested with weighted fusion. 2) Test: config_027 changes only aggregation relative to the best configuration, swapping avgpool for transformer. This checks whether weighted fusion lets the transformer aggregator work better than it did under concat. 3) Why this is the best final experiment: only the best accuracy counts, so the last run should go to the option with a realistic chance of beating 0.721. Every other untested choice changes a component (encoder or backbone) that has clearly underperformed. Transformer aggregation's poor result comes from a single run, so it is the least settled of those weak components. Isolating it on the strongest setup is the best remaining shot at exceeding 0.721, even though it is more likely to fall short.

1. Evidence: no experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion helps. 2. Test: config_001 (RNA-only, single profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest configuration in the space. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 that later results can be compared against. Each follow-up can then change one factor from this point: profile setting with config_002 or config_003, RNA encoder with config_004 or config_007, image modality with config_010, and fusion with config_016. That keeps the effect of each design choice separable. 3. Why now: with 10 experiments, an early simple reference is the cheapest way to cut uncertainty and avoid over-reading results from complex multimodal or multiprofile models. It also tests whether a simple model is already competitive, since added complexity is not guaranteed to help.

1) Evidence: The only result so far is the single-profile RNA baseline (PCA-2000), with accuracy 0.573 and F1 0.573. We do not yet know how informative the image modality is by itself, and that is the biggest open question about the search space. 2) Test: config_010 runs the single-profile image-only model with ResNet50 under the same setting as config_001. Only the modality changes, so the result gives a clean RNA-vs-image comparison. 3) Why now: About two-thirds of the remaining configurations are multimodal or image-based. Knowing whether images are competitive, complementary, or weak will tell us whether to spend the remaining 8 experiments on image encoders and fusion or on RNA encoders and multiprofile aggregation. One result will not settle this, but it sharpens later decisions more than tuning RNA settings first.

1) Evidence: two single-profile baselines so far. RNA-only with pca_n2000 (acc 0.573) clearly beats image-only with resnet50 (acc 0.422). Neither the profile setting nor fusion has been tested yet. 2) Test: config_016 adds resnet50 image features to the same pca_n2000 RNA setup using simple concat fusion, staying single-profile. Both encoders are unchanged from the tested baselines, so the only difference is combining the two modalities. This isolates whether adding the weaker image modality helps or hurts relative to the 0.573 RNA-only result. 3) Why now: whether multimodal fusion adds value is the design question that splits most of the remaining configurations, and the experiment is cleanly controlled against both completed runs. Its answer will decide whether to spend the remaining 7 runs on multimodal variants (multiprofile aggregation, weighted fusion, other encoders) or on RNA-only refinements such as scvi, scgpt and multiprofile aggregation.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only with PCA (0.573) is the best result so far. Image-only ResNet50 is much weaker (0.422). Concat fusion of the two (0.542, F1 0.483) did worse than RNA alone, so the image signal currently seems to add noise rather than help. Profile setting has not been tested at all, and it could be a large lever. 2. What this tests: config_002 keeps the best configuration fixed (RNA-only, PCA n2000) and changes only singleprofile to multiprofile, using simple avgpool aggregation. This isolates the effect of the profile setting without confounding it with encoder or fusion changes. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: multiprofile applies across most of the remaining search space, so its effect should be established early. If it helps, later experiments can test transformer aggregation and alternative RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) in the multiprofile setting. 1. Evidence: RNA carries most of the signal so far. RNA-only single-profile PCA gave the best accuracy (0.573 accuracy, 0.573 F1). Image-only ResNet50 was much weaker (0.422). Adding ResNet50 images via concat fusion lowered accuracy (0.542), with a larger drop in F1 (0.483). Moving to multiprofile avgpool also lowered results (0.540). The largest untested factor is the RNA encoder, since only PCA has been tried. 2. Test: config_004 swaps PCA for scVI in the best setup (RNA-only, single-profile) and changes nothing else. This isolates the effect of RNA representation on the strongest branch. 3. Why now: RNA representation looks like the main lever, so it is the most likely route to a higher best accuracy. The result also tells us which RNA encoder to carry into later aggregation or fusion experiments. scGPT (config_007) is the natural follow-up if scVI does not beat PCA.

1) Evidence: RNA is clearly the dominant modality. RNA-only PCA singleprofile is best at 0.573 accuracy. Image-only ResNet50 reaches only 0.422. Adding images by concat (0.542) and multiprofile avgpool (0.540) both lowered accuracy. Among RNA encoders, PCA beat scVI (0.507), but scGPT is still untested, so the RNA encoder choice remains the largest open question. 2) Test: config_007 changes only the encoder to scGPT, keeping RNA-only and singleprofile. This isolates the encoder effect against the current best. 3) Why now: if scGPT beats PCA, it would likely carry into the remaining multimodal and aggregation tests and could set a new best. If it loses, PCA is confirmed as the base. Then the last 3 experiments can go to weighted fusion (config_017) or transformer aggregation (config_003) built on PCA.

1) Evidence: RNA-only PCA single-profile (config_001, 0.573 accuracy) is the best result so far. The scVI and scGPT encoders, avgpool multiprofile and concat multimodal fusion all fell short of it. Concat fusion with ResNet50 (config_016) dropped to 0.542 and had a much lower F1 (0.483). The weak image branch (0.422) may be diluting the RNA signal. 2) Test: config_017 keeps config_016 identical and changes only the fusion from concat to weighted. This isolates whether a learned weighting can down-weight the weaker image modality and recover or beat RNA-only performance. 3) Why now: fusion is a key untested design choice, and the answer decides whether the remaining budget should go to multimodal variants (for example ViT-L or multiprofile weighted fusion) or to RNA-only refinements such as transformer aggregation (config_003). It is a clean one-variable comparison with real upside.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_017 (single-profile, PCA RNA + ResNet50, weighted fusion) at 0.586 accuracy and 0.574 F1. Weighted fusion clearly beat concat (0.542), and PCA was the strongest RNA encoder. The weak link looks like the image branch: ResNet50 image-only reached only 0.422, and the ImageNet ViT-L encoder has not been tested at all. Multiprofile avgpool lowered RNA-only accuracy (0.540 vs 0.573), so moving to multiprofile looks less promising right now. 2. Test: Keep everything from the best configuration and change only the image encoder to ViT-L. This isolates whether a stronger image representation raises multimodal weighted-fusion accuracy. 3. Why now: It is a single-variable extension of the current best, so it exploits the strongest direction while also answering an untested representation question. The result will guide the last two experiments, for example whether to pair the better image encoder with transformer aggregation.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_017 (PCA + ResNet50, singleprofile, weighted fusion) at 0.586 accuracy and 0.574 F1. Weighted fusion clearly beat concat with the same encoders (0.586 vs 0.542). PCA was the strongest RNA encoder, and ResNet50 far outperformed ViT-L when fused. The main open question is aggregation. Multiprofile avgpool hurt RNA-only accuracy (0.573 to 0.540), but transformer aggregation, which can learn to weight informative profiles instead of averaging them, has not been tested anywhere. 2. Test: config_021 keeps the best encoders and fusion fixed. It changes only the profile setting to multiprofile with transformer aggregation (these two choices come together, since aggregation only applies to multiprofile). This shows whether learned aggregation over multiple profiles can improve on the best singleprofile multimodal model. 3. Why now: with only two experiments left, exploiting the strongest direction while probing the one untested design dimension gives the best chance of a new maximum. Running the RNA-only transformer test (config_003) first would isolate the effect more cleanly, but it is unlikely to beat 0.586 itself. If config_021 underperforms, the final experiment can fall back to other variants around config_017.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_021 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.635 accuracy and 0.618 F1. Transformer aggregation appears to be the main driver of the multiprofile gain, because avgpool multiprofile hurt RNA-only (0.540 vs 0.573). PCA beat scVI and scGPT, and ResNet50 beat ViT-L by a wide margin, so swapping encoders is unlikely to help. The open question is fusion under multiprofile: concat trailed weighted in single-profile (0.542 vs 0.586), but that was without a learned aggregator.
